title: 2 Chronicles 24:17–27
context: After Jehoiada's death, the princes of Judah win Joash's ear, and the people abandon the LORD's house for Asherah poles and idols. God sends prophets, but they will not listen. When Zechariah son of Jehoiada rebukes them by the Spirit of God, they stone him in the temple court at the king's command. Within a year a small Syrian force defeats Judah's large army, Joash is wounded, and his own servants kill him for the blood of Jehoiada's sons. This parallels 2 Kings 12:17–21, which tells the Syrian episode and the conspiracy differently and does not record Zechariah's death.

verses.text: Now after the death of Jehoiada, the princes of Judah came and bowed down to the king. Then the king listened to them.
verses.arminianNotes: After Jehoiada's death the princes bow to the king, "then the king listened to them." Arminian readers note that Joash freely chooses new counselors, and that faith borrowed from a mentor must become one's own.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the turn comes immediately after Jehoiada's death. The Chronicler shows how much Joash's outward faithfulness had depended on another's influence.

verses.text: They abandoned the house of the LORD, the God of their fathers, and served the Asherah poles and the idols, so wrath came on Judah and Jerusalem for this their guiltiness.
verses.arminianNotes: They abandon the LORD's house and serve Asherah poles and idols, "so wrath came on Judah." Arminian readers see a national choice to turn away, with consequences that follow from it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the stark reversal: the house Joash restored is now abandoned. God's wrath answers covenant unfaithfulness, a pattern the Chronicler traces repeatedly.

verses.text: Yet he sent prophets to them to bring them again to the LORD, and they testified against them; but they would not listen.
verses.arminianNotes: "Yet he sent prophets to them to bring them again to the LORD." Arminian readers see God's patient pursuit of a rebellious people, giving real opportunities to return that they refuse.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that God's mercy precedes judgment. The prophets' testimony leaves the people without excuse, "but they would not listen."

verses.text: The Spirit of God came on Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest; and he stood above the people, and said to them, “God says, ‘Why do you disobey the LORD’s commandments, so that you can’t prosper? Because you have forsaken the LORD, he has also forsaken you.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The Spirit of God comes on Zechariah son of Jehoiada: "Because you have forsaken the LORD, he has also forsaken you." Arminian readers see covenant reciprocity, warning that turning from God brings real loss.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the Spirit-given word echoes earlier warnings in Chronicles. The son of the priest who saved Joash now speaks God's word to him and to the people.

verses.text: They conspired against him, and stoned him with stones at the commandment of the king in the court of the LORD’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: They stone Zechariah "at the commandment of the king in the court of the LORD's house." Arminian readers grieve that a prophet is killed for faithfully speaking God's word, and by the king's own order.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the sober gravity of the setting: blood shed in the court of the house Joash had restored. The narrator states the act plainly and lets its weight rest on the king.

verses.text: Thus Joash the king didn’t remember the kindness which Jehoiada his father had done to him, but killed his son. When he died, he said, “May the LORD look at it, and repay it.”
verses.arminianNotes: Joash "didn't remember the kindness which Jehoiada his father had done to him." Zechariah's dying words are, "May the LORD look at it, and repay it." Arminian readers see ingratitude and an appeal to God's justice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that many readers connect Jesus' words about "the blood of Zachariah" (Matthew 23:35; Luke 11:51) with this event, though Matthew's "son of Barachiah" raises a question interpreters discuss.

verses.text: At the end of the year, the army of the Syrians came up against him. They came to Judah and Jerusalem, and destroyed all the princes of the people from among the people, and sent all their plunder to the king of Damascus.
verses.arminianNotes: At the year's end the Syrians come, destroy the princes, and send plunder to Damascus. Arminian readers note that the princes who led Joash astray are among the first to fall.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 2 Kings 12:17–18 tells of Hazael's threat and Joash sending the temple treasures to buy him off. The two accounts describe the Syrian episode differently, and the difference is left standing.

verses.text: For the army of the Syrians came with a small company of men; and the LORD delivered a very great army into their hand, because they had forsaken the LORD, the God of their fathers. So they executed judgment on Joash.
verses.arminianNotes: A small Syrian company defeats a very great army, "because they had forsaken the LORD." Arminian readers see the reversal of the usual pattern as God's response to Judah's choice to forsake him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the Chronicler states that "the LORD delivered" Judah into Syrian hands, and that "they executed judgment on Joash." God governs the outcome of battle according to covenant faithfulness.

verses.text: When they had departed from him (for they left him seriously wounded), his own servants conspired against him for the blood of the sons of Jehoiada the priest, and killed him on his bed, and he died. They buried him in David’s city, but they didn’t bury him in the tombs of the kings.
verses.arminianNotes: His servants kill Joash on his bed "for the blood of the sons of Jehoiada," and he is not buried in the tombs of the kings. Arminian readers see the bitter harvest of his choices.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 2 Kings 12:20–21 places the killing at the house of Millo and says he was buried with his fathers in David's city. The burial details differ between the accounts and are not harmonized here.

verses.text: These are those who conspired against him: Zabad the son of Shimeath the Ammonitess and Jehozabad the son of Shimrith the Moabitess.
verses.arminianNotes: The conspirators are Zabad son of Shimeath the Ammonitess and Jehozabad son of Shimrith the Moabitess. Arminian readers note that the Chronicler records their foreign mothers, though the text does not say why.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 2 Kings 12:21 names them Jozacar son of Shimeath and Jehozabad son of Shomer. The names differ in form, and the difference is noted rather than resolved.

verses.text: Now concerning his sons, the greatness of the burdens laid on him, and the rebuilding of God’s house, behold, they are written in the commentary of the book of the kings. Amaziah his son reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes: His sons, the burdens laid on him, and the rebuilding of God's house are in "the commentary of the book of the kings." Arminian readers note that his reign is remembered for both its good beginning and its sad end.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the Chronicler cites a source not otherwise preserved. Joash's story stands as a sober warning that a good start must be followed by perseverance in faithfulness.
